title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps
authors: Torkel E Loman, Alexander P Browning, Ruth E Baker
abstract: In many differential equation models of real-world systems, the mechanistic structure of the dynamics is known, but the map from the dynamics to the observations is not. This is potentially problematic, as it can prevent us from e.g. learning model parameter values from data. Examples where this occurs include measuring a fluorescent marker as a proxy for the dynamics of a cellular circuit, and using wastewater measurements to follow the development of an epidemic. The nascent field of hybrid modelling, in which machine learning components (like neural networks) are embedded within mechanistic models, provides the tools to learn such maps. Here, the system's dynamics keep their mechanistic form, while a neural network represents the unknown observation map and is trained alongside any unknown core system parameters. This raises a question of identifiability: when can the true observation map be learnt, and when does one simply learn some map that transforms the dynamics into the available data? Building on previous work, we show how structural functional identifiability analysis can establish whether a model's unknown observation maps and core system parameters are identifiable, i.e. can be uniquely learnt from data. We both prove general results on when models with unknown observation maps are, and are not, identifiable, and demonstrate a general methodology (based on differential algebra) for assessing the identifiability of such models. This paves the way for applying classic differential equation workflows to the many real-world systems that contain such unknown maps.

infographic.key_insight: Structural functional identifiability analysis can determine whether unknown observation maps and mechanistic parameters can be uniquely recovered from data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps engineers assess whether hybrid mechanistic–neural models can recover meaningful sensor mappings and system parameters rather than merely fit observations.
method: Represent unknown observation maps with neural networks while preserving mechanistic differential equations.
Analyze map and parameter identifiability using differential algebra.
Prove general conditions for identifiability and non-identifiability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results and a general analysis methodology, but provides no quantitative benchmarks or dataset-level evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: Structural identifiability does not guarantee reliable recovery from noisy, finite data or successful neural-network training.
infographic.paper_title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps

title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
authors: Sergei Iudin, Mikhail Podobrii, Dmitry Zheltkov, Stanislav Moiseev
abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

infographic.key_insight: U(1)-symmetric tensor trains enable constraint-aware combinatorial search, with expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware sampling improving solution quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical approach to discrete optimization with hard linear constraints, where feasible solutions may be too rare for conventional sampling.
method: Represent constrained search spaces using U(1)-symmetric tensor networks.
Enhance expressibility when constructing sparse symmetric tensors.
Guide training-sample selection with a graph-based diversity measure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Assignment benchmarks show improved mean solution quality and separate runtime speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES; the diversifying strategy also improves nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains in higher-tensor-rank data families.
infographic.watch_item: Performance advantages are workload-dependent: runtime gains are reported for non-degenerate assignments, while comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget.
infographic.paper_title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains

title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
authors: Jingrun Chen, Yixin Luo, Xiaojun Peng
abstract: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

infographic.key_insight: A kernel-method analysis bounds RFM approximation and estimation errors through operator eigenvalues, linking convergence to activation regularity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory helps assess how random-feature count, collocation-observation count, and activation smoothness constrain RFM accuracy for linear PDEs.
method: Relate finite-feature approximation in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm to kernel ridge regression.
Bound RKHS estimation error from finitely many noiseless collocation observations.
Combine lower bounds and derive algebraic or stretched-exponential eigenvalue upper bounds from activation regularity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical upper and lower bounds under stated assumptions, but no numerical benchmarks or datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The estimation analysis assumes noiseless collocation observations; robustness to noisy data is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs

title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
authors: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

infographic.key_insight: Turing Agent coordinates theorem and proof formalization to turn research-level mathematical arguments into machine-verified knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its modular verification workflow offers a pattern for scaling trustworthy AI-generated proofs through decomposition, parallel checking, and reusable proof experience.
method: Separate theorem formalization and proof formalization agents.
Decompose proofs into auxiliary claims and verify them in parallel.
Reuse accumulated proof experience and selectively review semantic fidelity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports approximately 57–62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused RLMEval subset using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
infographic.watch_item: Machine-checked correctness still depends on faithfully translating the intended theorem; evaluation is concentrated in theoretical computer science.
infographic.paper_title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research

title: Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons
authors: Xinhao Yao, Zhenxing Dou, Yong Liu
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, yet the learning benefits of longer trajectories may not scale proportionally with their computational cost. We investigate how supervision utility evolves with trajectory length. Controlled experiments reveal diminishing returns from additional supervised tokens, while showing that later positions remain learnable and exhibit substantial cross-position supervision transfer. Gradient analysis further identifies shared update components across response positions and diverse position-specific residuals whose cross-rollout consistency decreases at greater depths. Motivated by these findings, we propose Stochastic Horizons On-Policy Distillation (SH-OPD), which reduces redundant supervision by randomly varying rollout horizons while preserving access to deeper response states. SH-OPD samples a shared horizon for each training batch, enabling efficient parallel generation without per-sequence horizon scheduling overhead. We characterize the resulting reweighting bias and derive a compute-reweighting trade-off under standard optimization assumptions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that SH-OPD achieves slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of the per-update cost of standard OPD, while maintaining competitive code generation performance at around 60% of the baseline cost. These results highlight the benefits of efficient supervision allocation across response depths.

infographic.key_insight: Longer on-policy distillation trajectories show diminishing supervision returns; randomizing rollout horizons reduces redundant work while retaining access to deeper response states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Stochastic Horizons On-Policy Distillation (SH-OPD) lowers per-update compute cost while preserving batch-parallel generation and competitive reasoning performance.
method: Analyze supervision utility, cross-position transfer, and gradient structure across response depths.
Sample one shared rollout horizon per training batch instead of supervising uniformly long trajectories.
Characterize horizon-induced reweighting bias and derive a compute–reweighting trade-off.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of standard OPD’s per-update cost and competitive code generation performance at around 60% of baseline cost.
infographic.watch_item: Random horizons reweight supervision across response depths; lower per-update cost does not by itself establish lower total training cost.
infographic.paper_title: Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons

title: Regularized Score Centering
authors: Hao Bai, Chenlu Ye, Xuanchang Zhang, Aviral Kumar, Tong Zhang
abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

infographic.key_insight: Regularized Score Centering stabilizes asynchronous reinforcement learning by constraining policy drift with a reverse-KL penalty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RSC targets instability from stale-policy data and training–inference numerical mismatch, improving sample efficiency in asynchronous agent training.
method: Use score centering to remove reward-baseline effects from expected updates.
Add reverse-KL regularization between learner and behavior next-token distributions.
Optionally apply truncated importance sampling to cap token importance weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations span dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks; RSC with TIS leads across six agentic tasks, reporting a 14.3% improvement on AppWorld and 9.9× the strongest baseline’s score on BabyAI.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation must track behavior-policy probabilities and tune regularization; the abstract does not specify computational overhead or sensitivity to these choices.
infographic.paper_title: Regularized Score Centering

title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality
authors: Shukai Du, Thu Le, Samuel N. Stechmann
abstract: High-dimensional function approximation is often subject to the curse of dimensionality, commonly described by a hypercube scaling regime with a large expense of $R^d$ grid points, where $R$ denotes the side length of a hypercube in $d$ dimensions. Here we show that a second scaling regime, which we call the lattice ball scaling regime, also arises and is relevant for practical applications. In this regime, the expense scales as $d^{R^2}/(R^2!)$ and therefore grows polynomially with $d$. This regime arises without additional special assumptions of special types of function spaces or error norms. The lattice ball scaling regime occurs when $R^2\ll d$, due to the discrete nature of counting the expense as the number of lattice points inside a hypersphere. Here we investigate this regime, which arises from the classical problem of approximating high-dimensional functions from common spaces of analytic or $m$-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal series (spectral method) such as Fourier, Chebyshev, and Legendre polynomial series. For many applications, the expense in the lattice ball scaling regime can be substantially smaller than that of the hypercube scaling regime, making accurate approximations more accessible. Numerical illustrations include classifying images of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset and learning the solution operators of partial differential equations, such as Burgers' equation and the radiative transfer equation. The potential for connections with artificial neural networks and other machine learning methods is also discussed.

infographic.key_insight: High-dimensional function approximation has a lattice-ball regime with cost scaling as d^(R²)/(R²!), polynomial in dimension d for fixed R, rather than the familiar hypercube cost R^d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: When R² ≪ d, this regime can substantially reduce spectral approximation costs without requiring special function spaces or error norms.
method: Approximate analytic or m-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal spectral series.
Study Fourier, Chebyshev, and Legendre expansions through lattice-point counting inside hyperspheres.
Identify the discrete lattice-ball scaling regime when R² ≪ d.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical illustrations on MNIST digit classification and solution-operator learning for Burgers’ and radiative transfer equations, but gives no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Polynomial scaling assumes fixed R; if the approximation scale required for accuracy grows with dimension, the cost advantage must be reassessed.
infographic.paper_title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality

title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
authors: Zihao Guo, Zhongmin Qian
abstract: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Activations inspired by the Biot–Savart kernel improve incompressible-flow PINNs without changing their velocity–pressure formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Flow-informed activations offer a targeted way to improve neural fluid solvers, including their resolution of localized shear structures.
method: Extract a smooth rational activation profile from a regularized Biot–Savart kernel.
Test fixed and learnable kernel-scale variants.
Retain conventional physics-informed training to isolate the activation’s influence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five flow benchmarks and 21 benchmark–architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduced combined velocity error versus tanh PINNs, with mean relative reductions of 31.7% and 33.2%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report computational overhead or establish generalization beyond the tested benchmarks and architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
authors: Xuan Zhang, Zhijian Zhou, Zicheng Hu, Yan Feng, Hongyan Hao, Yuan Qi
abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

infographic.key_insight: MCTS can waste exploration on differently worded versions of the same reasoning strategy; learned pseudo-counts let related branches share exploration evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Changing only UCT’s exploration statistic offers a targeted way to improve LLM reasoning search without redesigning the full search algorithm.
method: Identify count fragmentation caused by assigning independent visit counts to textual branches.
Use a lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on policy hidden representations to estimate representation coverage.
Replace standard UCT exploration counts with learned pseudo-counts in LPC-MCTS.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 5 math and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS outperformed strong MCTS baselines; inference-only count replacement with fixed LPC-MCTS-trained policies improved average mean@16 math accuracy by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 on Qwen3-4B.
infographic.watch_item: The reported inference-only gains use LPC-MCTS-trained policies, so they do not establish equivalent gains from a drop-in replacement on arbitrary pretrained policies.
infographic.paper_title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
authors: Maor Farid
abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

infographic.key_insight: Language models exhibit nonlinear dynamics across three clocks—network depth, training steps, and generated tokens—linking behaviors such as instability and repetition to established dynamical-systems concepts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reduced-order dynamical models offer interpretable tools for studying training stability and choosing generation temperatures that balance coherence with escape from repetition.
method: Synthesize about 200 papers into a Three-Clock Dictionary, labeling correspondences as proved, measured, or conjectured.
Derive mechanical and statistical models of softmax, gradient descent, attention, loss spikes, and repetition loops.
Test predictions on open language models using a laptop CPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on GPT-2 and Pythia support Arrhenius-law escape from repetition with logit-gap barriers; Pythia layers become more expansive during training, while a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability.
infographic.watch_item: Escape-based controllers remove repetition loops but do not yet outperform the best fixed temperature, and not all proposed dynamical correspondences are proved.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation

title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Yuming Zhang, Xianchen Zhou, Hongxia Wang
abstract: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.

infographic.key_insight: Amplifying constraint-aligned signals already present in trained denoisers improves candidate rankings before greedy decoding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PISG offers a training-free inference enhancement for diffusion-based routing and graph optimization solvers without requiring downstream refinement.
method: Construct a structure-degraded prediction at each denoising step.
Extrapolate the unperturbed prediction away from the degraded prediction.
Apply constrained greedy decoding to the guided scores.
infographic.evidence_signal: Without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 tested TSP solver-scale pairs and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to 4.8%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify inference overhead, and gains after 2-opt persist in most—not all—large-scale settings.
infographic.paper_title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
authors: Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, Peng Chen
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

infographic.key_insight: For nonlinear PDEs, a first-order least-squares residual can reliably measure solution error in the PDE-compliant norm under stability and regularity conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a principled training loss and inference-time error indicator for neural PDE surrogates without requiring labeled solutions for residual-based training.
method: Prove local residual–error equivalence using linearized stability and Lipschitz continuity of the residual derivative.
Verify conditions for monotone reaction, nonlinear diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity.
Train a finite-element reduced-basis neural operator using library-assembled losses and symbolic gradients; use solution snapshots only to build the basis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show that the square root of loss excess tracks error with factors comparable to the linear case, while the operator outperforms grid-based baselines in the PDE-compliant norm.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on equation-specific stability and regularity, may hold only near a solution branch, and can require control in a stronger norm.
infographic.paper_title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

title: CompCert4Lean: Porting a Verified C Compiler to Lean in Six Weeks with Parallel Coding Agents
authors: Cong Wang, Zhiyang Chen, Fan Long, Martin Rinard
abstract: We present CompCert4Lean, a large-scale port of CompCert 3.17's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean, completed in approximately six weeks by one expert directing parallel LLM agents. Our migration workflow partitions the development along its dependencies, audits translated definitions and theorem statements before large-scale proof reconstruction, and then reconstructs proofs in parallel against stable interfaces. The resulting compiler covers typed CompCert C through x86-64 assembly, discharges all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms, and produces executable Linux binaries. The workflow enabled the expert to concentrate on organizing the work rather than supplying technical solutions. Of 1,071 human interactions, 88.8% concerned workflow and coordination, while only three supplied technical direction. Optimization campaigns further demonstrate the benefit of the Lean port for agent-driven verified development. Under matched budgets of 24 active hours, GPT-6-astra produced a Lean candidate with 11.7% lower generated-program runtime across 29 small-tests programs, compared with 2.3% lower for its Rocq candidate, both relative to original CompCert 3.17 and while preserving the end-to-end correctness theorem. These results show that parallel LLM agents can support large-scale migration with limited human technical direction and subsequently improve the migrated compiler while retaining its formal guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: One expert directing parallel LLM agents ported CompCert’s verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean in approximately six weeks while retaining formal correctness guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Dependency-aware agent workflows can support large verified-software migrations and subsequent compiler optimization with limited human technical direction.
method: Partition the migration along dependency boundaries.
Audit translated definitions and theorem statements before reconstructing proofs.
Rebuild proofs in parallel against stable interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The port discharged all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms; under matched 24-active-hour budgets, agent-produced Lean and Rocq candidates reduced generated-program runtime by 11.7% and 2.3%, respectively, across 29 small-tests programs.
infographic.watch_item: Performance results cover only 29 small-tests programs, so gains may not generalize to larger production workloads.
infographic.paper_title: CompCert4Lean: Porting a Verified C Compiler to Lean in Six Weeks with Parallel Coding Agents

title: Structure-Preserving Neural Time-Stepping for Gradient-Flow PDEs via Onsager's Variational Principle
authors: Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You, Tao Zhou
abstract: We propose a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping (ONTS) framework for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the proposed framework employs spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely, the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, we develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme (E-ONTS), an implicit variational scheme (I-ONTS), and a predictor--corrector scheme (PC-ONTS) that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions. Furthermore, we rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen--Cahn, Cahn--Hilliard, Fokker--Planck, and coupled Poisson--Nernst--Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework.

infographic.key_insight: Learning rates or fluxes instead of solution states enables neural time-stepping that preserves key gradient-flow structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports physically consistent PDE simulation through mass conservation and conditionally guaranteed energy decay.
method: Use spatial neural networks to approximate Onsager rates for nonconserved dynamics and fluxes for conserved dynamics.
Advance solutions with explicit least-squares, implicit variational, or predictor–corrector schemes.
Guarantee discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundaries and unconditional energy stability for implicit schemes satisfying a descent criterion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on heat, Allen–Cahn, Cahn–Hilliard, Fokker–Planck, and coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck equations demonstrate accuracy, robustness, and structure preservation.
infographic.watch_item: Implicit energy stability requires satisfying a suitable descent criterion; it is not automatic for arbitrary neural optimization outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Structure-Preserving Neural Time-Stepping for Gradient-Flow PDEs via Onsager's Variational Principle

title: Physics-informed neural network for model-based global computation of the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators
authors: Petar Mircheski, Hiroya Nakao
abstract: The asymptotic phase is the central object of phase reduction theory for limit-cycle oscillators. It is a scalar coordinate defined throughout the basin of attraction of a limit cycle that advances at a constant natural frequency along every trajectory. Computing the phase from a given mathematical model requires solving a first-order partial differential equation (PDE) over the entire basin, which is challenging due to high computation costs and complex boundary conditions. In this study, we propose a physics-informed neural network to efficiently calculate the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators. By incorporating three types of loss functions, we train a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to satisfy the governing PDE for the asymptotic phase and the adjoint equation for the phase gradient. The trained network delivers the phase function accurately and, via automatic differentiation, allows the calculation of the phase gradient governing the oscillator's response to perturbations, which enables rapid entrainment closed-loop control using strong inputs. We validate the approach using three types of limit-cycle oscillators and demonstrate that the PINN can facilitate fast and global phase-locking control.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network learns the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators across their basin of attraction, enabling phase-based control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The learned phase and its gradient support rapid phase-locking control of modeled oscillators, including control with strong inputs.
method: Train a PINN with three loss types enforcing the phase PDE and the adjoint equation for its gradient.
Use automatic differentiation to obtain the phase gradient from the trained network.
Apply the learned phase information to closed-loop entrainment control.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on three types of limit-cycle oscillators and demonstrations of fast, global phase-locking control, but provides no quantitative error or runtime metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Global accuracy should be checked across the intended basin, since satisfying sampled physics constraints does not by itself guarantee accurate phase estimates everywhere.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-informed neural network for model-based global computation of the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
authors: Zhaosong Lu, Yifeng Xiao
abstract: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

infographic.key_insight: An inexact SVRG method improves first-order oracle complexity for constrained convex finite-sum optimization while guaranteeing constraint violation at most ε and expected optimality gap at most ε.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets applications with hard constraints and may be especially useful when constraint gradients and cone projections are cheaper than objective gradients.
method: Use inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient updates.
Target ε-surely feasible stochastic optimal solutions, not merely feasibility in expectation.
For a single objective function, specialize to a deterministic first-order method for convex conic optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved theoretical complexity bounds and preliminary numerical results, but provides no benchmark details or quantitative outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: Practical gains depend on the relative costs of objective gradients, constraint gradients, and cone projections.
infographic.paper_title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization

title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
authors: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Chunyuan Zheng, Yanyi Li, Cong Fang
abstract: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

infographic.key_insight: Colombo is a self-organizing AI research system that studies oracle-based optimization by jointly advancing achievable algorithmic guarantees and lower bounds on unavoidable costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its complexity results can help engineers assess whether optimization methods efficiently use a prescribed information interface and where further improvements remain possible.
method: Map known guarantees, lower bounds, and unresolved gaps in a living Complexity Atlas.
Adapt research plans and reciprocally challenge algorithms with hard problem families.
Check claims through independent review and Lean-based formal certification, retaining findings in long-term memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty Atlas settings, but provides no detailed evaluation or certification coverage.
infographic.watch_item: Assess the assumptions and formal-certification coverage of individual results before applying them to practical optimization problems.
infographic.paper_title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization

title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity
authors: Teng-Yuan Chang, Gung-Min Gie, Youngjoon Hong, Chang-Yeol Jung
abstract: We develop neural network methods for the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations at a small viscosity $\varepsilon > 0$, whose accuracy is uniform in $\varepsilon$ and whose residual is evaluated on a grid that does not resolve the vorticity boundary layer. In the vorticity-stream function formulation with the slip boundary conditions, a vorticity layer of width $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ forms along the walls. The trial function of the singular layer Physics-Informed Neural Network (sl-PINN) contains the corrector of the asymptotic analysis, together with the law that fixes its amplitude at the wall. The amplitude is tied to the wall trace of the network itself, so that the method requires no a priori knowledge of the limit solution. The sl-PINN keeps the error uniform in $\varepsilon$ over six decades, for the Stokes and the Navier-Stokes equations alike, although in the latter the wall trace travels with the flow and is not known in advance. An enrichment that uses the thin scale but leaves the profile and the amplitude of the layer free deteriorates as $\varepsilon\to0$. Since the corrector carries the layer analytically, the Laplacian in the residual can be discretized by a finite volume flux difference on a coarse grid. The resulting singular layer Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) attains the same uniform accuracy as the sl-PINN, to within the scatter of the random seed, at about half the cost of a training step. The combination of the asymptotic corrector with the coarse-grid finite volume discretization is the main result of this article.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding an asymptotic boundary-layer corrector in neural trial functions preserves accuracy as viscosity decreases, without requiring a grid that resolves the thin vorticity layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables coarse-grid neural solutions of small-viscosity flow problems, with a finite-volume variant costing about half as much per training step.
method: Use the vorticity–stream function formulation of 2D incompressible flow with slip boundary conditions.
Embed the asymptotic layer profile and tie its amplitude to the network’s wall trace, avoiding prior knowledge of the limit solution.
Replace the residual’s Laplacian evaluation with coarse-grid finite-volume flux differences in sl-FVNN.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports viscosity-uniform accuracy across six decades for Stokes and Navier–Stokes tests, with sl-FVNN matching sl-PINN within random-seed scatter.
infographic.watch_item: The reported results concern 2D flows with slip boundaries; extension to other boundary conditions requires appropriate correctors and validation.
infographic.paper_title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity

title: Variance Stable Gaussian Smoothing Estimator for Arbitrary High-order Derivatives
authors: Shuixin Fang, Xuerui Wang, Hang Zeng, Tao Zhou
abstract: Computing high-order partial derivatives in high dimensions by automatic differentiation can be costly in both computation and memory. Stein's identity offers an alternative through Gaussian smoothing, but the variance of the resulting estimators can diverge as the step size tends to zero, even with antithetic sampling. We propose a variance stabilization technique that extends antithetic sampling from a reflection pair to $n$ equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane. Under local analyticity, we prove that, when $n$ is at least the derivative order, the bias is of order $O(σ^n)$ and the variance remains bounded as the smoothing step size $σ$ tends to zero. Numerical experiments support these predictions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the estimator in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for polyharmonic and Cahn--Hilliard equations. The technique mitigates the bias-variance trade-off in smoothing-based derivative estimation and is useful for PINNs solving high-order partial differential equations.

infographic.key_insight: Replacing antithetic reflection pairs with equally spaced complex-circle samples stabilizes Gaussian-smoothing estimates of high-order derivatives as the step size shrinks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The estimator offers an alternative to costly high-order automatic differentiation for PINNs solving high-order partial differential equations.
method: Estimate derivatives using Stein’s identity and Gaussian smoothing.
Extend antithetic sampling to n equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane.
Under local analyticity and n at least the derivative order, obtain O(σ^n) bias and bounded variance as σ approaches zero.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments support the theoretical predictions and demonstrate effectiveness in PINNs for polyharmonic and Cahn–Hilliard equations.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require local analyticity, and implementation requires evaluating the target function at complex-valued inputs.
infographic.paper_title: Variance Stable Gaussian Smoothing Estimator for Arbitrary High-order Derivatives

title: From Constraints to Causality: Petri net Encodings for Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
authors: Alex Chan, Mohamed Tarraf, Alex Yakovlev, Rishad Shafik
abstract: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained hardware and on-device components in autonomous systems. However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. Finally, we outline two directions this opens: a correctness-of-translation theorem, and a causal-trace analysis of where two trained BNNs diverge in their decisions, a structural question that constraint-based verifiers cannot express.

infographic.key_insight: Encoding a fixed, trained Binary Neural Network as a 1-safe Petri net makes inference steps explicit, yielding causal traces of how predictions arise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This representation could help engineers inspect decision changes in resource-constrained, safety-relevant systems beyond checking input-output properties.
method: Compositionally translate BNN inference semantics into a 1-safe Petri net.
Represent computation steps as transitions and inference executions as firing sequences.
Contrast firing sequences to localise where a single-feature change alters the prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: A worked example demonstrates exhaustive input-output equivalence with a reference implementation and trace-based localisation of a prediction change.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to a worked example; a general correctness-of-translation theorem and cross-model trace analysis remain future work.
infographic.paper_title: From Constraints to Causality: Petri net Encodings for Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
